**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I saw the name *Elias Voss* carved into the oak door of the old bookshop, I knew it wasn’t just a name. It was a promise—or a warning. The shop had been in his family for three generations, according to the faded plaque beside the door, and the air inside smelled of aged paper, beeswax, and something sharper: the scent of secrets. I’d come for the rare first edition of *The Shadow of the Wind*, but the moment I stepped inside, I realized I was looking for something else.

Elias was behind the counter, sorting through a stack of dog-eared novels, his fingers moving with the precision of a man who had spent a lifetime turning pages. He was tall, with dark hair streaked with silver at the temples, and eyes the color of storm clouds. When he looked up, I saw the way his gaze lingered—not on my face, but on the book I clutched to my chest like a shield.

“You’re not the first to ask for that,” he said, his voice low, like the hum of a distant engine. “But you’re the first to look like you know what you’re getting into.”

I swallowed. “What do you mean?”

He didn’t answer right away. Instead, he reached under the counter and pulled out a leather-bound volume, its cover worn smooth by time. *The Black Library of Lost Souls*, the title read in ink that had bled slightly with age. “This,” he said, sliding it across the counter, “is what happens when you chase books that aren’t meant to be read.”

My pulse quickened. “You’re saying it’s cursed?”

A ghost of a smile touched his lips. “I’m saying it’s dangerous. And you, my dear, have the look of someone who doesn’t believe in danger.”

I should have walked out then. I should have laughed and told him he was full of it. But the book in my hands was warm, almost pulsing, and when I opened it, the pages were blank—except for the last one, where a single sentence had been written in a handwriting that wasn’t mine:

*“You took it. Now you must give back what was stolen.”*

Elias watched me, his expression unreadable. “Did you see that?”

I nodded, my voice barely a whisper.

He exhaled sharply. “Then you understand.”

“Understand what?”

“That some stories aren’t meant to be read. Some names aren’t meant to be spoken. And some doors,”—he gestured to the one behind him—“aren’t meant to be opened.”

I should have listened. But I was already reaching for the handle.

The moment I turned it, the door groaned like a living thing. The shop around me shifted—shelves rearranged themselves, books whispering as they slid into place. And then I saw it: a figure standing in the far corner, cloaked in shadow, its face obscured by a hood. It raised a hand, and the air between us rippled like water.

“You shouldn’t have come,” the figure said, its voice like dry leaves skittering across stone.

Elias stepped forward, his voice cutting through the unease. “Elias Voss doesn’t make mistakes.”

The figure tilted its head. “Then why are you here?”

Because I was afraid. Because I was curious. Because sometimes, the things we’re told not to do are the only things worth doing.

And because, for the first time in my life, I believed in names.

The last thing I remember is the way the book in my hands burned like ice. The last thing I hear is Elias’s voice, urgent and low:

*“Run.”*

But it’s too late.

The door slams shut behind me.

And the name on my lips is no longer mine to keep.

---

**The End.**

*(Or is it?)*
